image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated scatter/segment plot with arrows and a trend line**
- It shows many diagonal line segments/arrows positioned over time, plus a single fitted **trend line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- Uses **overlaid line segments/arrows** for individual observations
- Uses **color highlighting** to emphasize selected leaders versus many muted background cases
- Includes **text annotations/labels** for selected individuals
- Includes a **trend line** across the full panel

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date leaders took office | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Age at taking office | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Individual leader (e.g., Truman, Reagan, Merkel, Trump, Biden) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to selected line segments/arrows |
| Leader/observation identity | Categorical/nominal | Separate line segment/arrow mark for each observation |
| Highlight/group status (selected vs background; also different highlight colors) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (red, blue, gray/light gray) |
| Overall time trend in age | Quantitative summary over time | Black trend line |

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that there seems to be a clear negative trend in the ages of world leaders, over the past 70 years. In 1950, the average age of world leaders seemed to be around 62, whereas in 2020, it seems to have dropped to around 52.  The spread in ages of world leaders does not seem to have changed though, as the spread appears to be around 20 years above and below the average across all years. Another thing I noticed is that Republican U.S. presidents appear to generally be older than Democrat U.S. presidents, as most of the republican presidents are above the trend line and most democrat presidents are below the trend line in age. 
I wonder why Republican presidents tend to be older than Democrat presidents, and I also wonder if there are distinct differences in ages based on parties for other countries. I wonder what may explain these differences in age based on party affiliation, and if age could somehow be correlated to presidential election winners based on party. I also wonder if the trend line is statistically significant in the model.
This impacts my community and me as it shows that in general, world leaders have been younger and younger over the years, as this could perhaps impact who a candidate may relate to most. 
“Changes in Average Ages of World Leaders Over Time”

I personally believe that adults of all ages can successfully lead nations. However, I would like more young leaders in the government; we need leaders that understand our generation and what we care about. The youth are constantly coming up with new and innovative ways to improve upon our world, and we need to be seen in the government. We also need to have leaders with diverse experiences and backgrounds, so the country can be a better place for everyone, not just certain groups.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  "Our Leaders Are the Grandparents of Nations" by Frank of Milford, Delaware, “Presidents: Old and Experienced, or Young and Innovative?“ by Sam of Academy of Saint Elizabeth, "Are the Older Bolder, or Will They Smolder?" by Bella of USA, "Age Is Just a Number, But Does It Influence the President?" by Sophie of Andover, Massachusetts, and “Are US Presidents Too Old?” by Morgan of Tulsa, Oklahoma.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow afternoon Thursday, Oct. 29 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

I noticed that Churchill was the oldest in office, while Kennedy was the youngest in office. If Biden were to be elected, he would be the oldest president entering office. I also notice that the majority of democratic presidents fall under the trend line (Truman doesn't), while republican presidents either cross or are past the trend line. Based on the gray arrows, it also seems like the youngest leader of a democratic nation is well below the age of forty, and the oldest leader of a democratic nation well over the age of eighty. 
I wonder why the average age has a downward trend, as shown by the trend line. I wonder how age relates - if at all - to the way that democratic leaders govern their nation. I also wonder whether age affects the nation's views of the president/PM, and if it plays in a role in voting. I wonder how this graph would compare if leaders of non-democratic nations were included. Since elected democrats tend to be younger than elected republicans, I wonder why that is. Is it because conservative and liberal ideals appeal differently between generations? 
This impacts my community because if age correlates to the decisions that leaders make in office, then if affects us, the population that they're governing. Younger candidates will appeal more to younger generations such as Gen Z and millennials and be lost in touch in with older generations such as Gen X and boomers.

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

The Presidential election is in six days.  There are so many graphs of polls and the positions of the candidates and their supporters.  Rather than a graph on these aspects of the election, here is a graph about the ages of O.E.C.D. (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) world leaders since 1950.  What is the trend of the ages of world leaders when they are in office?  And, how do the ages of our candidates compare to the  ages of recent world leaders?  

Here are a couple words you may want to check for your understanding and use in your response:  gerontocracy, ageism, Baby Boomers, and presidential vs. parliamentary systems.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Finally, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the graph. 

By Friday, we’ll reveal the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  Reply even after you have read the Reveal.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

Most Republican Presidents are above or on the trendline age. The oldest Republican Presidents were Reagan and Trump, with Bush being slightly older. This just creates a divide and continues to stir arguments between people because of the drastic age demographic representation.
